summary: Standardizes the media types application/xml, application/xml-external-parsed-entity, and application/xml-dtd, and defines text/xml variants as aliases. It also standardizes the +xml suffix. It obsoletes RFC 3023 and updates RFC 6839.

plainLanguage.summary: When an XML document is sent over the network, it is wrapped in a media type that says what it is. This RFC fixes those names, and it fixes the rule for working out which character set the document is in when the header and the document itself disagree: the byte order mark wins, then the header, then the declaration inside the document.

questions: what does +xml media type suffix mean
which encoding wins bom or charset
subtitle: Which MIME type labels an XML document, how its character encoding is decided, and what the +xml suffix means.

tldr.problem: XML documents travel over the network inside media entities, and both MIME and XML have their own way of saying which character set the bytes are in. When those two disagree, a receiver has to guess, and different implementations guess differently.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers application/xml, application/xml-external-parsed-entity and application/xml-dtd, defines text/xml and text/xml-external-parsed-entity as aliases, and sets a priority order for the three possible sources of encoding information: a byte order mark first, then the charset parameter, then the XML encoding declaration.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7303 is a Proposed Standard from July 2014 that obsoletes RFC 3023 and updates RFC 6839. It aligns the two text types with their application counterparts, adds XPointer fragment identifiers and XML Base, and registers the +xml structured syntax suffix for XML-based media types.

today: RFC 7303 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2014. It obsoletes RFC 3023 and updates RFC 6839, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The World Wide Web Consortium has issued the Extensible Markup Language (XML) 1.0 and XML 1.1 specifications. To enable the exchange of XML network entities, this specification standardizes three media types, application/xml, application/xml-external-parsed-entity and application/xml-dtd, two aliases, text/xml and text/xml-external-parsed-entity, and a naming convention for identifying XML-based MIME media types using the suffix '+xml'.

XML has been used as a foundation for other media types, including types in every branch of the IETF media types tree. To facilitate the processing of such types, and in line with the recognition in RFC 6838 of structured syntax name suffixes, a suffix of '+xml' is registered, so that generic XML-based tools such as browsers, editors and search engines can work with all XML-based media types.

This specification replaces RFC 3023. The major differences are the alignment of text/xml and text/xml-external-parsed-entity with application/xml and application/xml-external-parsed-entity respectively, the addition of XPointer and XML Base as fragment identifiers and base URIs, the integration of the XPointer Registry, and the updating of many references.
sections.plainLanguage: XML is used to build many kinds of data format, so a generic tool needs a quick way to recognise one. The naming convention gives it that: a type whose name ends in +xml is XML, and can be handed to an XML processor.

sections.title: Characters, Encodings and Charsets
sections.content:
Both XML, in an XML or Text declaration using the encoding pseudo-attribute, and MIME, in a Content-Type header field using the charset parameter, use a common set of labels to identify the MIME charset, which is the mapping from a byte stream to a character sequence. In this specification, the phrase charset parameter refers to whatever MIME charset is specified by a MIME charset parameter, and encoding declaration refers to whatever MIME charset is specified by an XML encoding declaration. The phrase character encoding, or simply encoding, is reserved for the MIME charset actually used in a particular XML MIME entity.

Unicode defines three encoding forms, UTF-8, UTF-16 and UTF-32. As UTF-8 can only be serialized in one way, the only possible label for UTF-8-encoded documents is 'utf-8'. UTF-16 XML documents can be serialized in one of two ways, either big-endian, labelled optionally 'utf-16' or 'utf-16be', or little-endian, labelled optionally 'utf-16' or 'utf-16le'. UTF-32 has four potential serializations, of which only UTF-32BE and UTF-32LE are given names; support for the various serializations varies widely and security concerns about their use have been raised. The use of UTF-32 is NOT RECOMMENDED for XML MIME entities.

Both MIME and XML have defined the term entity with different meanings. In MIME, the term refers specifically to the header fields and contents of either a message or one of the parts in the body of a multipart entity. In XML, an XML document may consist of one or many storage units called entities, which all have content and are all, except for the document entity and the external DTD subset, identified by entity name. In this specification, an XML MIME entity is defined as the latter, an XML entity, encapsulated in the former, a MIME entity. Where XML provides for naming and referencing entities for purposes of inclusion or substitution, the phrase XML-entity is used to avoid confusion.
sections.plainLanguage: Two words that sound alike mean different things here. A charset parameter is what the transport header says, an encoding declaration is what the document says about itself, and the encoding is whichever one is actually in force. MIME and XML also both use the word entity for different things, so this document calls the combination an XML MIME entity.

sections.title: Encoding Considerations
sections.content:
As many as three distinct sources of information about character encoding may be present for an XML MIME entity: a charset parameter, a byte order mark, and an XML encoding declaration. Ensuring consistency among these sources requires coordination between entity authors and MIME agents, that is, processes that package, transfer, deliver and receive MIME entities. The use of UTF-8, without a byte order mark, is RECOMMENDED for all XML MIME entities.

Some MIME agents are XML-aware, meaning they can process XML MIME entities as XML and detect the XML encoding declaration or its absence; all three sources of encoding information are available to them. Other agents are not XML-aware, so they cannot know anything about the XML encoding declaration, they lack one of the three sources of information, and they are less likely to be aware of this specification. Some agents, such as proxies and transcoders, both consume and produce MIME entities.

For producers, XML-aware MIME producers SHOULD supply a charset parameter and/or an appropriate byte order mark with non-UTF-8-encoded XML MIME entities that lack an encoding declaration, and SHOULD remove or correct an encoding declaration that is known to be incorrect, for example as a result of transcoding. XML-aware MIME producers MUST supply an XML text declaration at the beginning of non-Unicode XML external parsed entities that would otherwise begin with the hexadecimal octet sequences 0xFE 0xFF, 0xFF 0xFE or 0xEF 0xBB 0xBF, in order to avoid the mistaken detection of a byte order mark. XML-unaware MIME producers MUST NOT supply a charset parameter with an XML MIME entity unless the entity's character encoding is reliably known, which is particularly relevant for the central configuration of web servers, where configuring a default for the charset parameter will almost certainly violate this requirement. XML MIME producers are RECOMMENDED to provide means for users to control what value, if any, is given to charset parameters, for example by giving users control of the configuration of filename to Content-Type header mappings on a file-by-file or suffix basis.

For consumers, the question of priority arises when the available information is not consistent. When a charset parameter is specified, the normative component of the XML specification leaves open how to determine the encoding with which to attempt to process the entity, and in particular does not say which is authoritative when in-band information conflicts with the charset parameter. This specification sets the priority as follows: a byte order mark is authoritative if it is present in an XML MIME entity, and in the absence of a byte order mark the charset parameter is authoritative if it is present. Whenever the above determines a source of encoding information as authoritative, consumers SHOULD process the entity based on that information.

When producers conform to the requirements stated above, inconsistencies do not arise, so the priority statement only has practical impact for non-conforming entities. In the face of inconsistencies, no uniform strategy can deliver the right answer every time; the purpose of specifying one is to encourage convergence over time, first on the part of consumers and then on the part of producers. For XML-aware consumers, the XML specification does not make it an error for the charset parameter and the XML encoding declaration, or the UTF-8 default, to be inconsistent, although such consumers might choose to issue a warning. If the charset parameter is omitted, no information is being provided about the character encoding by the Content-Type header: XML-aware consumers MUST follow the requirements in the XML specification for that case, and XML-unaware consumers SHOULD NOT assume a default encoding.
sections.plainLanguage: Three things can say what encoding a document uses, and they can disagree. The rule is simple: a byte order mark at the start of the document wins, and if there is none, the header wins. The declaration inside the document is used only when neither of the other two is present.

sections.title: Which Media Type for Which XML Entity
sections.content:
Within the XML specification, XML MIME entities can be classified into four types, called document entities, external DTD subsets, external parsed entities and external parameter entities. The appropriate usage for the registered types is as follows. For document entities, the media types application/xml or text/xml, or a more specific media type, SHOULD be used. For external DTD subsets, the media type application/xml-dtd SHOULD be used, and the media types application/xml and text/xml MUST NOT be used. For external parsed entities, the media types application/xml-external-parsed-entity or text/xml-external-parsed-entity SHOULD be used, and the media types application/xml and text/xml MUST NOT be used unless the parsed entities are also well-formed document entities. For external parameter entities, the media type application/xml-dtd SHOULD be used, and the media types application/xml and text/xml MUST NOT be used.

RFC 3023, which this specification obsoletes, recommended the use of text/xml and text/xml-external-parsed-entity for document entities and external parsed entities respectively, but described handling of character encoding that differed from common implementation practice. These media types are still commonly used, and this specification aligns the handling of character encoding with industry practice. The obsolete RFC 2376 allowed application/xml and text/xml to be used for any of the four types, although in practice it was likely to have been rare.

Neither external DTD subsets nor external parameter entities parse as XML documents, and while some XML document entities may be used as external parsed entities and vice versa, there are many cases where the two are not interchangeable. XML also has unparsed entities, internal parsed entities and internal parameter entities, but they are not XML MIME entities.

Compared with the earlier documents, this specification alters the handling of character encoding of text/xml and text/xml-external-parsed-entity, treating them no differently from the respective application types. The application types are still RECOMMENDED, to avoid possible confusion based on the earlier distinction. The former confusion around the question of default character sets for the two text types no longer arises, because RFC 7231 changes RFC 2616 by removing the ISO-8859-1 default and not defining any default at all, and RFC 6657 updates RFC 2046 to remove the US-ASCII default.
sections.plainLanguage: XML has four kinds of thing that can be sent, and they are not interchangeable: whole documents, external DTD subsets, external parsed entities and external parameter entities. The RFC says which media type to use for each, and in particular that the plain application/xml type must not be used for the DTD kinds.

sections.title: The +xml Suffix
sections.content:
When a new media type is introduced for an XML-based format, the name of the media type SHOULD end with '+xml' unless generic XML processing is in some way inappropriate for documents of the new type. This convention allows applications that can process XML generically to detect that the entity is supposed to be an XML document, verify the assumption by invoking an XML processor, and then process the document accordingly. Applications may check for types that represent XML MIME entities by comparing the last four characters of the subtype to the string '+xml', although four of the five media types defined in this specification also represent XML MIME entities while not ending in '+xml'.

Media types following the naming convention SHOULD define the charset parameter for consistency, since XML-generic processing treats all XML MIME entities uniformly as regards character encoding information. There are cases where the parameter need not be defined: when an XML-based media type is restricted to UTF-8, because UTF-8 is the default for XML, and when it is restricted to UTF-8 and UTF-16, because neither UTF-8 nor UTF-16 requires an XML encoding declaration.

XML generic processing is not always appropriate. Authors of some media types may wish the types to remain entirely opaque except to applications specifically designed for them, and by not following the '+xml' convention they can avoid XML-generic processing. Since generic processing will be useful in many cases, including in some situations that are difficult to predict ahead of time, the convention is to be preferred unless there is a particularly compelling reason not to use it. The registration process for specific '+xml' media types is described in RFC 6838, and new XML-based media type registrations in the IETF must follow these guidelines. When other organisations register XML-based media types through the Specification Required policy, the relevant Media Reviewer should ensure that they use the '+xml' convention so that interoperability of their XML-based documents is maximized. Only media subtypes that represent XML MIME entities are allowed to register with a '+xml' suffix. The change controller has been changed to the World Wide Web Consortium.
sections.plainLanguage: A media type for XML-based data should normally end in +xml, so that any XML tool can recognise it. The exceptions are types meant to stay opaque to general XML processing, and types limited to UTF-8, where the parameter is unnecessary.

sections.title: Fragment Identifiers, Base URI and XML Versions
sections.content:
URIs can contain fragment identifiers, and RFC 3986 devolves the syntax and semantics of fragment identifiers to the media type registration. The syntax and semantics for the XML media types defined here are based on the XPointer Framework W3C Recommendation, which allows simple names and more complex constructions based on named schemes. When the syntax of a fragment identifier part of any URI or IRI with a retrieved media type governed by this specification conforms to the XPointer Framework syntax, conforming applications MUST interpret such fragment identifiers as designating whatever is specified by the XPointer Framework together with any other specifications governing the XPointer schemes used that the applications support. Conforming applications MUST support the 'element' scheme as defined in XPointer Element, but need not support other schemes. If an XPointer error is reported, this specification does not define an interpretation for the part. A registry of XPointer schemes is maintained at the W3C, and generic processors of XML MIME entities SHOULD NOT implement unregistered XPointer schemes.

An XML MIME entity of type application/xml, text/xml, application/xml-external-parsed-entity or text/xml-external-parsed-entity MAY use the xml:base attribute to embed a base URI in that entity, for use in resolving relative URI references. The base URI itself might be embedded in a different MIME entity, since the default value for the xml:base attribute can be specified in an external DTD subset or external parameter entity. Since conforming XML processors need not always read and process external entities, the effect of such an external default is uncertain, so its use is NOT RECOMMENDED.

The five media types are to be used with the XML specification. Where the examples show a version attribute of 1.0, it is understood that 1.1 might also appear, provided the content does indeed conform to XML 1.1. The normative requirement of this specification upon XML documents and processors is to follow the requirements of the XML specification, Section 4.3.3. Specifications and recommendations based on or referring to this RFC SHOULD indicate any limitations on the particular versions or editions of XML to be used.
sections.plainLanguage: A link can point inside an XML document, and this RFC says how: with XPointer, the W3C scheme for naming a piece of a document. A document can also carry its own base address, so that relative links inside it resolve correctly.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC provides registrations for the five media types and for the '+xml' naming convention. The registration of application/xml has no required parameters and an optional charset parameter, with the details in Section 3. Its encoding considerations say that depending on the character encoding used, XML MIME entities can consist of 7bit, 8bit or binary data. For 7-bit transports, 7bit data such as US-ASCII-encoded data does not require content-transfer-encoding, but 8bit or binary data such as UTF-8 or UTF-16 data MUST be content-transfer-encoded in quoted-printable or base64. For 8-bit clean transports such as 8BITMIME ESMTP or NNTP, 7bit or 8bit data does not require content-transfer-encoding, but binary data such as UTF-16 MUST be content-transfer-encoded in base64. For binary clean transports such as BINARY ESMTP or HTTP, no content-transfer-encoding is necessary, or even possible in the case of HTTP.

The interoperability considerations record that XML has proved to be interoperable across both generic and task-specific applications and for import and export from multiple XML authoring and editing tools, and that validating processors provide maximum interoperability because they have to handle all aspects of XML, although a non-validating processor may be more efficient. In practice, character set issues have proved to be the biggest source of interoperability problems, and the use of UTF-8 together with careful attention to the guidelines of Section 3 is the best way to avoid them.

The additional information for application/xml records that there is no magic number, although XML MIME entities in ASCII-compatible character sets often begin with the hexadecimal 3C 3F 78 6D 6C, that is, the four characters that open an XML declaration, and those in UTF-16 often begin with the same characters encoded in UTF-16, with or without a byte order mark. The file extension is .xml and the Macintosh file type code is 'TEXT'. The same structure is given for the other four registrations, and the '+xml' structured syntax suffix is registered in its own section, with the change controller moved to the World Wide Web Consortium.
sections.plainLanguage: The registrations spell out how each type should be sent over different kinds of transport, because a text-only link cannot carry raw UTF-16 bytes. The RFC also notes that character set confusion, not the XML itself, has been the main source of interoperability problems with XML on the network.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
XML MIME entities contain information that may be parsed and further processed by the recipient. These entities may contain, and recipients may permit, explicit system level commands to be executed while processing the data. To the extent that a recipient application executes arbitrary command strings from within XML MIME entities, they may be at risk.

In general, any information stored outside the direct control of the user, including CSS style sheets, XSL transformations, XML-entity declarations and DTDs, can be a source of insecurity. For example, a small whiteout attack modification made to a master style sheet could make words in critical locations disappear in user documents, without directly modifying the user document or the style sheet it references. The security of any XML document is therefore vitally dependent on all of the documents recursively referenced by that document. The XML-entity lists and DTDs for XHTML 1.0 are likely to be a widely exploited set of resources, used and trusted by many developers, few of whom will know much about the level of security on the W3C's servers or on any similarly trusted repository.

The simplest attack involves adding declarations that break validation. Adding extraneous declarations to a list of character XML entities can effectively break the contract used by documents, and a small change that produces a fatal error in a DTD could halt XML processing on a large scale. Extraneous declarations are fairly obvious, but more sophisticated tricks, such as changing attributes from being optional to required, can be difficult to track down. Perhaps the most dangerous option available to attackers, when external DTD subsets or external parameter entities or other externally specified defaulting is involved, is redefining default values for attributes: if developers have relied on defaulted attributes for security, a relatively small change might expose enormous quantities of information.

Another option, XML-entity spoofing, can be used to insert text into documents, vandalizing and perhaps conveying an unintended message. Because XML permits multiple XML-entity declarations, and the first declaration takes precedence, it is possible to insert malicious content where an XML-entity reference is used.

Security considerations will vary by domain of use, and XML may also have some of the same security concerns as plain text, including escape sequences that, when displayed, can change the display processor environment in ways that adversely affect subsequent operations.
sections.plainLanguage: An XML document can pull in other documents, and the danger is often in those: a shared DTD or style sheet can be changed to break or to alter every document that uses it. The RFC points at that risk, because it is the documents an author does not control that cause the trouble.

viz.caption: THE THREE SOURCES OF ENCODING INFORMATION, IN ORDER OF PRIORITY

items.title: 1. Byte order mark
items.text: Authoritative if present at the start of the entity. It is a signature, not part of the document.

items.title: 2. Charset parameter
items.text: Authoritative when there is no byte order mark. It comes from the Content-Type header.

items.title: 3. XML encoding declaration
items.text: Used when neither of the others is present, in the shape the XML specification requires.

items.title: Recommended
items.text: Use UTF-8 with no byte order mark for all XML MIME entities.

items.title: UTF-32
items.text: NOT RECOMMENDED. Support varies widely and security concerns have been raised.
